mcqs.question: A store holds 1TB of logical data with a replication factor of 3. How much physical storage does the cluster actually need, and why does this matter for capacity planning?
options: 1TB — replication factor doesn't affect total stored bytes
2TB — only 2 of the 3 replicas count toward billable storage
3TB — every replica is a full physical copy, so replication multiplies both storage and per-node request load
1TB, but split across 3x as many nodes
mcqs.explanation: Each replica is a complete physical copy, so a replication factor of 3 means roughly 3TB stored, not 1TB — and this multiplier also inflates per-node request load, not just disk usage. There's no partial-counting of replicas, and splitting across more nodes doesn't reduce total bytes stored.

mcqs.question: Why does a consistent-hashing ring place each physical node at many virtual positions instead of just one?
options: It makes hashing computationally faster
It is required to support the delete operation
It reduces the total number of physical nodes needed
It spreads a failed or joining node's keyspace impact evenly across many other nodes instead of concentrating it on one neighbor
mcqs.explanation: With only one ring position per physical node, that node's entire arc dumps onto a single neighbor on failure; virtual nodes scatter that arc across many nodes, smoothing the impact. Virtual nodes don't speed up hashing itself, don't relate to delete semantics, and don't reduce the physical node count needed.

mcqs.question: A shopping-cart service needs read-your-writes consistency for a user's own cart. Which R/W/N configuration guarantees that?
options: R + W > N
N = 1 with no replication
W = 0, fire-and-forget writes
mcqs.explanation: R + W > N guarantees any read set overlaps with the most recent successful write's replica set, giving read-your-writes. R=1,W=1 is fast but can miss the latest write; N=1 removes durability entirely; W=0 doesn't even confirm the write landed anywhere.

mcqs.question: A celebrity's profile key is hashed evenly onto the ring like any other key, yet its owning node is overloaded. What does this tell you?
options: The consistent-hashing implementation has a bug
The replication factor N is set too low
Consistent hashing balances storage by key count, not access frequency, so a hot key can overload its node regardless of even hash distribution
Vector clocks are missing for that key
mcqs.explanation: Consistent hashing evenly distributes keys by hash value, not by how often each key is accessed — a single very popular key can overload its node even with perfectly even key distribution. This isn't a bug, isn't fixed by changing N, and has nothing to do with conflict-resolution mechanisms like vector clocks.

mcqs.question: Why does rebalancing with plain `hash(key) % N` cause far more data movement than a consistent-hashing ring when a node joins?
options: Modulo hashing reassigns nearly every key's owner whenever N changes, while a ring only reassigns the keys in the new node's arc
Modulo hashing is slower to compute per key
Modulo hashing cannot support replication
Consistent hashing avoids using a hash function entirely
mcqs.explanation: Because `% N` changes for almost every key when N changes, modulo hashing triggers a near-total reshuffle; a ring's structure confines the change to one node's arc. The issue isn't raw compute speed, and both approaches can support replication — consistent hashing still uses a hash function, just structured differently.
